hook.text: Zara produces 450 million garments a year. The average item is worn seven times before being discarded.

buildup.text: Fast fashion emerged in the 1990s when brands shortened production cycles from months to weeks.

discovery.text: Fashion is the second most polluting industry after oil. It produces 10% of global carbon emissions.

twist.text: The Rana Plaza collapse in 2013 killed 1,134 garment workers. The brands they sewed for denied all responsibility.

climax.text: Consumers want cheap clothes but ethical production. These demands contradict each other at every price point.

punchline.text: Cheap clothes are expensive—someone else just pays.

quiz.question: How many people died in the Rana Plaza collapse?

details.summary: Fast fashion delivers trendy clothing at rock-bottom prices by externalizing costs onto workers and the planet. The industry produces 100 billion garments annually, with 60% discarded within a year. Behind every $5 shirt lies exploitation, pollution, and waste on a staggering scale.
details.whyItMatters: Fast fashion's true cost is hidden from consumers. Understanding its environmental destruction and labor exploitation is essential for making informed clothing choices.
takeaways: Fashion is the second most polluting industry after oil
The Rana Plaza collapse in 2013 killed 1,134 garment workers
The average garment is worn only seven times before disposal

faq.question: How did fast fashion become so dominant?
faq.answer: Brands like Zara and H&M pioneered ultra-rapid production cycles, delivering runway-inspired designs to stores in weeks rather than months. Globalization moved manufacturing to low-wage countries, dropping prices dramatically.

faq.question: What happened at Rana Plaza?
faq.answer: On April 24, 2013, an eight-story garment factory in Bangladesh collapsed, killing 1,134 workers. Workers had reported cracks in the building the day before but were ordered to continue working. The disaster exposed the deadly conditions behind cheap clothing and prompted industry safety reforms.
